attrs.numbers_show: Receivables grew 101.5% ($26.7M to $53.8M) while revenue grew 58.4% ($118.2M to $187.3M); DSO rose from 82 to 105 days (E23). attrs.verdict: explanation does not fit the numbers

attrs.reason: Management attributes the working capital increase to revenue growth driving higher receivables (E33). However, receivables grew 101.5% ($26.7M to $53.8M) while revenue grew only 58.4% ($118.2M to $187.3M), and DSO rose from 82 to 105 days (E23). Quarterly signals show revenue growth decelerating each quarter (Q1 +108%, Q2 +79%, Q3 +46%, Q4 +31%) while receivables growth accelerated (Q1 +64%, Q2 +92%, Q3 +101%, Q4 +102%) and DSO surged in H2 (Q3 63→87, Q4 61→94 days) (E25-E28). The named driver (revenue growth) is too small to explain the receivables pattern; the DSO expansion points to extended terms or shipment timing not corroborated by any reported mix-shift data in the pack.

rebuttal.innocent_explanation: The receivables growth exceeding revenue growth reflects a shift toward distributor channels with longer payment terms and a year-end stocking surge by distributors ahead of FDA regulatory uncertainty (E30). The quarterly signals show a timing effect in Q4 where receivables grew 102% vs revenue 31% (E28), consistent with large December shipments on extended terms. Management's working capital comment (E33) correctly notes that the net working capital increase was modest because the receivables buildup was offset by cash used for share repurchases (a financing outflow), not that share repurchases affected CFO. The CFO stagnation (E24) is explained by the operating asset increase (receivables) consuming cash, which is consistent with the numbers.

attrs.final_verdict: explanation does not fit the numbers
